claims.text: A market brings buyers and sellers into contact for exchange of a particular good or service; it need not be a physical place. Marketing is the management process which identifies consumer wants and anticipates their future wants. It guides decisions about how an offering meets those wants through product, price, promotion and distribution. Research collects information and advertising communicates promotional messages; both can contribute to the wider marketing role but neither is its complete definition. Good marketing connects understanding customers with a feasible offering, rather than merely persuading people to buy whatever has already been made.

claims.text: A business identifies customer needs through relevant research, sales patterns, feedback and observation. It then decides which customers to serve and designs a suitable product or service, price and access. A stated preference is not a guaranteed sale: affordability, competing products and the buying situation matter. Test a feasible offering and use feedback to improve it. Customer focus does not require accepting every request at any cost. A change must fit resources and earn sufficient revenue for the enterprise’s purpose. Customer needs can change, so an initial survey does not remove the need to review actual behaviour.

claims.text: Marketing objectives can include increasing sales, increasing market share, attracting new customers, retaining existing customers, developing awareness and supporting a successful new-product launch. They should fit wider business aims and available resources. State a result, not just an activity: running an advertisement is an action, whereas increasing awareness among a defined target group is an objective. A measurable target and time period make review possible. More sales are not automatically more profit if the cost of achieving them exceeds the added return.

claims.text: Market segmentation divides a market into groups of consumers with similar needs. The syllabus bases include product, region, purpose, price, age and gender. Segments can overlap: buyers in one region can also seek budget-priced products for a particular purpose. Use evidence that the chosen grouping affects needs rather than assuming all people in a demographic category behave alike. Assess potential demand, purchasing ability, competition, reach and whether the business can serve the segment with its resources. A small enterprise may focus on a niche instead of trying to offer everything to everyone, but excessive dependence on a narrow group creates risk. A supported target decision links a real need with an achievable offering and recognises the strongest alternative.

claims.text: Market orientation means research identifies customer wants before the product is developed and produced. Product orientation starts from the product or the enterprise’s technical strengths and then seeks buyers for that offering. The distinction is what guides the offering first, not whether either business advertises. Market focus can reduce the risk of an unwanted offer but costs time and research can be imperfect. Product focus can support technical innovation and expertise, yet may miss what buyers can use or afford. A business can combine technical capability with customer evidence rather than ignoring one.
